title: Why the world’s first spinal cord transplant is so controversial
content:
A recent spinal cord transplant performed in Russia has sparked controversy due to a lack of supporting evidence for the procedure’s efficacy or timing. The operation, described as a world first, involved removing a section of spinal cord from a patient with a complete spinal cord injury and replacing it with a donor segment. While the source notes that details regarding the specific case are scant, it highlights that there is little evidence to suggest the surgery was successful or that the scientific groundwork was sufficiently established before the intervention.

The article contrasts this procedure with the historical development of the polio vaccine by virologist Jonas Salk. Salk is cited as an example of necessary medical risk-taking, noting that he tested his vaccine on cells, monkeys, and children who had already contracted polio before administering it to his own family. Although his approach deviated from modern standard protocols, the text argues that Salk took significant steps to mitigate risks, a level of caution not evidenced in the Russian spinal cord case.

Historical precedents are used to illustrate the dangers of acting ahead of medical evidence. The article references early synthetic organ transplants, specifically the replacement of tracheas with plastic tubes, which were implanted without adequate testing on large animals due to time constraints. These premature procedures resulted in complications and deaths. The text emphasizes that while randomised controlled trials are the gold standard for new medical procedures, alternatives like compassionate-use protocols exist for critically ill patients, as seen in current pig kidney transplant trials.

Ultimately, the piece argues that while courage and imagination are valuable in medical advancement, experimental surgeries require a solid foundation of science. The source concludes that the dream of spinal cord transplants may become a reality in the future, but only if the underlying scientific evidence is established first, rather than relying solely on the willingness to take untested risks.
summary: Shutterstock/PeopleImages The virologist Jonas Salk said that “hope lies in dreams, in imagination and in the courage of those who dare to make dreams into reality”. Salk was certainly daring – he risked paralysing himself, his wife and their children while testing his polio vaccine.
author: New Scientist

title: Artemis III SLS Core Stage Joins Boosters at Kennedy
content:
NASA technicians completed the integration of the Artemis III Space Launch System (SLS) core stage with twin solid rocket boosters on October 28, 2026, inside High Bay 3 of the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This assembly marked the completion of the rocket’s short stack configuration. Prior to this final step, the 212-foot core stage was moved from High Bay 2 to High Bay 3 using a unique lifting beam designed to position the stage onto the mobile launcher.

Following the integration, the assembly will undergo testing and checkouts. Once these procedures are finished, teams will roll the core stage and booster stack out to Launch Pad 39B. At the pad, a tanking test will be conducted where liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen fuel will be loaded exclusively into the core stage. During this phase, launch teams will also practice countdown procedures and timelines.

The Artemis III mission is scheduled to launch NASA astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, and Andre Douglas, along with European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano, aboard the Orion spacecraft. The primary objective of the mission is to test rendezvous and docking capabilities between the Orion spacecraft and commercial vehicles provided by Blue Origin and SpaceX. These tests are intended to support future missions aimed at landing astronauts on the Moon.
summary: NASA technicians integrated the Artemis III SLS core stage with twin solid rocket boosters in High Bay 3 at Kennedy Space Center to complete the short stack configuration. The mission will launch astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and Luca Parmitano aboard Orion to test rendezvous and docking capabilities before a future lunar landing.

title: MIT Tech Review: Context layer key for AI value
content:
MIT Technology Review Insights has released a report highlighting the disconnect between AI capabilities and their practical utility within enterprises. The publication notes that while many organizations deploy various AI tools, such as customer platforms and conversational assistants, the outcomes often lack proper business understanding. This gap is a primary reason companies struggle to achieve significant returns on their AI investments.

A poll conducted by MIT Technology Review Insights reveals that although every surveyed organization uses AI, only 16% are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The majority of respondents, 40%, report moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% cite meaningful gains. Conversely, 23% of organizations experience minimal or no returns. Current usage remains largely experimental, with 38% of companies piloting use cases and 35% using AI to assist employees via tools like co-pilots. Only 12% have AI agents in production, and 3% use AI to perform most work in key processes.

Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan, identifies the missing element as context, defined as how well AI understands a business. He describes a "context layer" as the architectural infrastructure that sits between business systems and AI platforms, translating enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents. Sankar argues that without this layer, AI is akin to a blindfolded smart intern thrown into an organization. He emphasizes that while artificial general intelligence is effectively present for real-life intents, it remains largely unuseful in most companies due to this lack of contextual integration.
summary: A poll by MIT Technology Review Insights found that only 16% of organizations are extracting transformative value from their AI deployments. Prukalpa Sankar of Atlan argues that a context layer is the missing architectural infrastructure needed to help AI understand enterprise business systems.
author: MIT Tech Review

content:
St. Lucie County officials have stated they will not investigate the ownership of a cluster of unpermitted Flock cameras that were removed during a countywide takedown effort. According to a report by The Washington Post, residents remain upset because they do not know who installed the devices or how the collected data was used. Hannah Galindo, a 31-year-old resident who petitioned for the cameras' removal, expressed concern that the data could be located anywhere.

The Post reported that of the twelve cameras discovered, five were claimed by city law enforcement. A Flock spokesperson told the publication that a police department mistakenly issued guidance allowing officers to post multiple cameras under a single permit, despite the county’s requirement for individual permits. Neither Flock nor the police departments in Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce, which claimed the cameras, will confirm who provided that guidance.
summary: St. Lucie County will not investigate who installed 12 unpermitted Flock cameras that were removed during a countywide takedown, and the cameras have since disappeared. Residents remain upset, and five cameras were claimed by city law enforcement, while a police department mistakenly issued guidance that officers could post multiple cameras under one permit.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google AI Gives Evasive Answers to 2020 Election Winner Question
content:
Google’s AI Mode has begun providing indirect responses to questions regarding the outcomes of the 2020 and 2024 United States presidential elections. When asked directly who won the 2020 election, the AI advised users to consult the Federal Election Commission (FEC) for official results, statistics, and winner certification, rather than naming the victor. Similar evasive answers were received for inquiries about the 2024 election, where the AI again directed users to the FEC for information.

In contrast, the AI provided a direct link to The American Presidency Project’s 2012 Data Center when asked about the 2012 election. For every other presidential election going back to 2000, the system offered detailed and correct responses identifying the winner. These observations follow reports of complaints on social media regarding the AI’s cagey answers to these specific recent electoral queries.
summary: If you ask some prominent US politicians who won the 2020 presidential election, you might get some weasely answers that fail to directly acknowledge Joe Biden's win that November. If you ask Google's AI Mode the same question, you might get an evasive answer that simply tells you to consult with outside sources.
author: Ars Technica

title: Cadillac Escalade IQ delivers 440‑mile range and 200‑kWh battery
content:
The Cadillac Escalade IQ, a large electric SUV, features a substantial battery pack containing over 200 kWh of lithium-ion cells. This capacity supports an impressive range, with Cadillac stating the vehicle achieves 460 miles (740 km) on the EPA test cycle. During a recent review, the vehicle arrived with an indicated range of 440 miles (708 km), a figure that made recharging unnecessary for a full week of testing. The model is designed to demonstrate that replacing a V8 engine with powerful electric motors does not compromise Cadillac’s ambitions, even as the brand plans to maintain a mix of electric and combustion vehicles beyond 2030.

The Escalade IQ shares its battery pack and other components with several other full-size General Motors electric vehicles, including the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the GMC Sierra EV, and the Hummer EVs. Like these models, the Escalade is characterized by its significant size and weight. Its curb weight is 9,046 lb (4,103 kg), which is approximately one-third heavier than the last gas-powered version tested. This mass places the vehicle in the Class 3 truck category, necessitating flat side mirrors and meaning there is no formal EPA range rating, despite the manufacturer’s claimed figures.

Despite the vehicle’s substantial weight, which exceeds four tons, it is equipped with numerous airbags. The Escalade is designed to be just small enough to fit into a standard parking space, balancing its large physical footprint with practical parking dimensions. The review highlights that the electric SUV’s primary advantage lies in its extensive range and the technological parity it shares with other GM full-size electric trucks and SUVs.
summary: Cadillac Escalade IQ delivers 440‑mile range and 200‑kWh battery.
author: Ars Technica

title: Amazon Adds Camera to Echo Studio Smart Speaker
content:
Amazon has released a new version of its Echo Studio that adds an integrated camera, calling it the Echo Studio with Home Camera. The update comes alongside a range of other Alexa‑enabled devices, but the speaker itself retains the same audio hardware as the original 2019 model.

Both versions of the Echo Studio feature a 3.75‑inch high‑excursion woofer, three full‑range drivers, Dolby Atmos support, and Amazon’s proprietary surround‑sound algorithm. They also provide lossless HD audio, Advanced Room Adaptation—which continuously tunes sound to a room’s acoustics— and noise‑distortion‑fighting features. Each unit houses a four‑mic array and the AZ3 Pro processor, which includes an AI accelerator for Amazon’s Alexa+ generative‑AI chatbot.

The primary new differentiator for the Echo Studio with Home Camera is the added camera, while its audio capabilities remain unchanged from the standard Echo Studio.
summary: Amazon Adds Camera to Echo Studio Smart Speaker.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Carbon, new frontier AI model not yet available
content:
Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its latest frontier AI model. The release comes just two weeks after the company launched Gemini 4 Argon. Unlike the expected Flash model, Carbon is described as an improvement on Argon, and Google is pursuing a staged release that may take time.

According to Google, Gemini 4 Carbon reaches a new threshold in coding, agentic tasks, and scientific analysis. The company says the model delivers a “significant leap” in vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation, and that it is twice as likely to generate code free of vulnerabilities compared with Argon. The Chrome team adds that Carbon is ten times better at producing high‑quality patches than non‑Google models.

Google also reports that Carbon has raised its score by 89 points on WebDev Arena, moving it to fourth place on the leaderboard. The model is not yet available for public use.
summary: Google has announced Gemini 4 Carbon, an improved version of Gemini 4 Argon that is not yet available for public use. The model reportedly achieves significant gains in coding, agentic tasks, scientific analysis, cybersecurity vulnerability detection, validation, remediation, and patch generation, and has increased its WebDev Arena score by 89 points to rank fourth.
author: Ars Technica

title: Blue Origin, SpaceX, Virgin Galactic All Pause US Space Tourism Missions
content: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon. But that was then. Consider the state of play today: It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs. SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth. As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024. So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States. Read full article Comments
summary: Blue Origin's New Shepard last flew in January and has been paused, while SpaceX's Dragon finished its final free‑flyer mission in April 2025 and will be retired. Virgin Galactic's final suborbital flight on VSS Unity occurred in June 2024, leaving the United States without a space tourism mission for 10 months.
author: Ars Technica

title: Trump Administration Sues Utah to Protect Kalshi from State Gambling Ban
content: The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets. Utah, which prohibits gambling, sued Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah's lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events. “Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.” Read full article Comments
summary: The Trump administration is suing Utah to stop the state from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the agency that regulates prediction markets. Utah sued Kalshi in state court last week, seeking an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.

content: Last week, two critical bugs in PHP, the open‑source language powering roughly 70 % of websites, forced organizations to scramble for fixes. Some sites were taken offline until the vulnerabilities could be patched, underscoring that the cleanup from the recent PHP scare is still underway.
summary: Two critical bugs in the PHP language, which powers roughly 70% of websites, emerged last week and prompted organizations to scramble to fix their systems. Wiz’s CTO warned that the issue could lead to a broader vulnpocalypse and noted that some sites were taken offline until patches were applied.

content: Microsoft announced that it has achieved its tenth consecutive quarter of record‑breaking revenue. The company reported quarterly earnings of $92.3 billion, marking a 19% increase over the same period a year earlier.

content: Microsoft reported that it earned $10 billion in revenue from commercial arrangements with OpenAI, including revenue‑sharing payments, in the quarter ending September 30. The figure underscores the significant financial dependency between the two companies.

title: Israel Election Night: Netanyahu Faces Worst Result Since
content:
Israel’s election night has delivered a series of unexpected developments. Ballots are still being counted in a vote that saw the highest turnout in decades, while Arab parties made historic inroads. Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest‑serving prime minister, recorded his worst electoral result since 1999, yet he still has a possible path to remain in power.

Analysts are now using calculators and pie charts to map the scenarios in which Netanyahu could survive. The focus is on whether the challenge lies with the right‑wing Likud leader himself or with his policies. The final composition of the next parliament will determine the outcome.
summary: Israel Election Night: Netanyahu Faces Worst Result Since.

title: Amid uncertainty over EU aid, Vitalii Kim insists Ukraine has no choice but to fight for motherland
content: François Picard is pleased to welcome Vitalii Kim, Minister for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine. “If Europe will not support us, we also will fight because it's our motherland,” says Kim, insisting that Ukraine's determination to resist Russian aggression will endure regardless of the outcome of negotiations over European financial assistance. Yet behind this assertion of national resolve lies a more complex reality: a country confronting not only the immediate pressures of war, but also its mounting psychological, social and institutional consequences.
summary: François Picard is pleased to welcome Vitalii Kim, Minister for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine. “If Europe will not support us, we also will fight because it's our motherland,” says Kim, insisting that Ukraine's determination to resist Russian aggression will endure regardless of the outcome of negotiations over European financial assistance.

title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil, lands in Florida by private plane
content:
Flavio Bolsonaro, the right‑wing presidential candidate who was defeated in Brazil’s runoff election, arrived in Florida by private plane on Wednesday. He fled the country after a Brazilian court ordered him to surrender his passport, a move he refused to comply with.

Bolsonaro lost the election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday. He is currently under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering, and his defeat means he will lose parliamentary immunity, according to FRANCE 24’s international affairs editor Kethevane Gorjestani.
summary: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil, lands in Florida by private plane.

title: Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw 9/11, Trump and Maduro cases, dies at 92
content: Alvin Hellerstein, a senior U.S. federal judge, died on Wednesday at the age of 92. He had overseen the trial against former Venezuelan president Nicholas Maduro, handled lawsuits related to the September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center, and presided over multiple cases involving former President Donald Trump.
summary: Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who oversaw 9/11, Trump and Maduro cases, dies at 92.

title: Arab-majority parties poised to win historic 19 seats in Israeli election
content:
Two Arab‑majority parties are projected to secure a combined 19 seats in Israel’s election, a result described as historic. The outcome comes as the country recorded a record voter turnout on Tuesday.

According to FRANCE 24’s Emerald Maxwell, the Arab‑Israeli electorate—descendants of Palestinians who remained after Israel’s creation and comprising roughly 20 percent of the population—has expressed anger toward the Netanyahu government’s ultra‑nationalist Jewish vision for Israel and the Palestinian territories.
summary: Two Arab-majority parties are set to win a historic 19 seats in total in the Israeli election. The outcome comes amid a record turnout and anger among Arab voters over the Netanyahu government's ultra‑nationalist Jewish vision for Israel and the Palestinian territories.

content:
A summit that includes nearly two dozen African leaders has opened in Moscow, with the Kremlin describing the participating countries as natural allies against the West.  

Nigerian investigators report that dozens of detained miners who died in a crowded jail cell screamed for help while jailors ignored their suffering.  

Ahead of the Youth Olympics in Senegal, Kenya is increasing its support for its women’s sportspeople.

Women journalists covering crises are confronting heightened threats, including online abuse, gender‑based attacks and a climate of impunity.

content: The new head of the UN World Food Programme, Luke Lindberg, said on Wednesday that reducing conflict is the single most effective way to tackle global hunger. He noted that conflict drives two‑thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide.

title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fall short of majority, coalition talks loom in Israel
content:
Coalition negotiations are expected to begin in Israel after election results showed that neither the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor the bloc headed by retired General Gadi Eisenkot secured a parliamentary majority. Projections indicated a surge in votes for Palestinian parties, contributing to the highest voter turnout in decades.

Analysts noted that the rise of Palestinian parties in the Knesset could reshape Israel’s political landscape. With Netanyahu’s governing majority lost, his future hinges on whether opposition Jewish parties are willing to form a coalition that includes the newly strengthened Palestinian groups.

Eisenkot, who leads the Jewish opposition bloc, signaled that he does not intend to join a broad coalition that incorporates Palestinian parties, declaring a “Zionist majority” in a premature statement of victory. This stance suggests that any governing arrangement will require further negotiations among the fragmented parties.
summary: Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs fall short of majority, coalition talks loom in Israel.

content: Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives At least 68 killed in Toledo train crash – full report Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville. “I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.

content: At a summit with African leaders in Moscow, President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s “genius” and said he was in touch with the controlling shareholder of Starlink. He noted that Russia is developing its own satellite‑communications system, the Rassvet constellation, and compared it with the Earth‑orbiting network built by Musk’s SpaceX. Putin said the Russian version is intended for military use against Ukraine, positioning it as a domestic alternative to Starlink.
summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin praised Elon Musk’s genius and said he was in touch with Starlink’s controlling shareholder. title: Bush Heritage raises $19m to buy Wooroora station in far north Queensland
content:
A conservation fundraiser has secured more than $19 million in private donations to enable Bush Heritage to purchase Wooroora Station in far north Queensland. The group aims to complete the acquisition by Christmas, protecting a tract of land that connects wet tropics and World Heritage rainforest and contains headwaters that flow toward the Great Barrier Reef.

Wooroora spans over 20,000 hectares of largely intact wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland on the lands of the Jirrbal people, roughly 100 km south‑west of Cairns. The property borders Bush Heritage’s existing 43,575‑hectare Yourka Reserve and provides habitat for 12 endangered species, reinforcing the biodiversity of one of Australia’s most species‑rich regions.
summary: Bush Heritage raises $19m to buy Wooroora station in far north Queensland.

title: US military releases clear photo of China's Shenlong space plane docked in orbit
content:
A U.S. military intelligence agency has released a new photograph of China’s reusable Shenlong space plane, capturing the spacecraft while it is docked to another satellite in orbit. The image was captured in 2024 by Vantor’s WorldView 3 satellite from a distance of 56 miles (90 kilometers). This satellite-based perspective provides a resolution of 4.5 centimeters (1.8 inches) per pixel, revealing details with greater clarity than previous ground-based observations of the spacecraft.

In the released image, the robotic Shenlong space plane is shown docked to an unidentified satellite that has its solar panels deployed. The photograph also shows Shenlong’s payload bay doors in an open position. Analysts suggest these open doors may provide clues regarding the activities of the space plane during its fourth mission, which launched in February 2026. While the specific satellite it was docked to remains unknown, the high-definition view offers new insights into the mysterious spacecraft.

China’s space agency has provided limited public information, stating only that Shenlong assists in testing technologies intended to pave the way for more convenient and affordable round-trip methods for the peaceful use of space. However, independent observations indicate the spacecraft has engaged in other activities while in orbit. In June 2026, American space intelligence company LeoLabs reported detecting a new object in the vicinity of the space plane. LeoLabs stated with high confidence that the object was released from the Chinese space plane, noting that this activity is consistent with sub-satellite deployments observed during previous missions.

Similar object releases occurred during Shenlong’s third mission, which ended in 2024, and its second mission in 2023. During the 2023 mission, the space plane may also have conducted proximity and rendezvous operations, where two spacecraft maneuver close to one another. It remains possible that the released objects were unnecessary hardware discarded before landing. Due to the military nature of the program, few operational details about Shenlong have been made public.

The United States also operates a secretive robotic space plane, the Boeing-built X-37B, and rarely releases concrete details about its capabilities or missions. In February 2025, the U.S. Space Force released its first photo of the X-37B in space, which appeared to show the craft in high Earth orbit with its payload bay doors open. Additionally, in 2023, the Space Force released an official painting depicting an X-37B-like space plane in orbit intercepting another satellite.

As China and the United States compete in what many observers describe as a new Space Race, these rare images may serve as a method for militaries and intelligence agencies to hint at their capabilities without fully disclosing them to the public.
summary: A US military intelligence agency released a high-resolution satellite image showing China's Shenlong space plane docked to another spacecraft with its payload bay doors open. The photograph, captured in 2024 by Vantor's WorldView 3 satellite, provides new details on the vehicle's fourth mission and its ability to release objects in orbit.
author: Space.com

title: Everest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questions over their lofty ambitions
content:
National Geographic’s documentary "Everest: The Other Side" offers an immersive portrait of mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they attempt to become the first people to ski down Mount Everest’s north face. With some screenings presented in the IMAX format, the film is described as evoking the spectacle and scale of early large-format cinema, though its intense focus on the climbers’ ascent and descent may provoke anxiety or vertigo for some viewers.

The narrative follows Morrison and Nelson as they plan and execute practice runs for their ambitious goal. The review notes that the film spends considerable time depicting the pair scaling the steep, less-traveled north face before skiing back down, a sequence that leaves the specific motivations for the descent inadequately explained. Morrison is characterized as an amiable experienced mountaineer who appears compelled to place himself in grave danger, a risk that could potentially endanger others involved in any necessary rescue efforts.

Hilaree Nelson shares her partner’s passion for the climb, and the first third of the film tracks their preparation for the expedition. The review highlights that neither climber seems able to fully articulate why they have chosen to take such significant risks. Nelson attempts to frame her mountaineering lifestyle as a personal career choice that her two teenage sons should accept, suggesting they might even thank her for it. This perspective is complicated by the reality that if she were injured or lost, her sons and Morrison—who is not the boys’ biological father—would be left to deal with the aftermath.
summary: The documentary follows mountaineers Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they seek to become the first people to ski down Everest's north face. The film presents an immersive portrait of their climb while raising moral questions about their risky ambitions and the potential impact on their family.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Metropolis: Street Photography 1985–2025 exhibition opens in Sydney
content:
The exhibition Metropolis: Street Photography 1985–2025 is currently on display at The Photographic Gallery in Sydney, running until 17 November. The collection documents over four decades of urban life, transitioning from the film-noir streets of 1980s New York to the period surrounding the fall of the Berlin Wall. It concludes with the modern, colour-saturated geometry of contemporary Australian streets, showcasing a range from classic monochrome grit to vivid colour abstraction.

The exhibition examines how photographers have captured the relentless energy of ever-changing cities. It serves as a celebration of unscripted characters, strange encounters, and the absurd comedy that emerges when people share public space.
summary: The exhibition spans four decades of street photography, transitioning from 1980s New York film-noir styles to contemporary Australian colour imagery. It showcases how photographers have documented the energy and characters of changing cities until 17 November at The Photographic Gallery, Sydney.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Danny Masterson Loses Rape Appeal, 30-Year Sentence Upheld
content:
Danny Masterson, the actor known for his role on That ’70s Show, has lost his appeal against his rape conviction, resulting in the upholding of his 30-year prison sentence. Masterson was convicted in 2023 of two counts of rape involving two women who were also Scientologists, with the offenses allegedly occurring in 2003. A third charge, relating to an alleged rape of a different plaintiff in 2001, was quashed. The appeal centered on Masterson’s argument that the judge was biased against Scientology.

The article notes that the two women against whom Masterson was convicted were members of the same religious group. While the source mentions the specific legal argument regarding judicial bias, it does not provide further details on the appellate court’s reasoning or the specific evidence presented during the original trial.

For individuals affected by rape or sexual abuse, the article lists several support resources. In the United States, RAINN can be reached at 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis provides support at 0808 500 2222. In Australia, assistance is available through 1800Respect at 1800 737 732. Additional international helplines are referenced via a link to ibiblio.org.
summary: Danny Masterson has lost his appeal against his rape conviction, resulting in the upholding of his 30-year prison sentence. The actor was convicted in 2023 of two counts of rape after arguing that the judge was biased against Scientology.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Melanie Lynskey Stars and Executive Produces Paramount+ Series 'Mushroom Murders'
content:
Melanie Lynskey, an Emmy-nominated New Zealand actor, has been cast as Erin Patterson in the new limited series Mushroom Murders: There’s More to Unearth. The Paramount+ production, which is slated to premiere in 2027, will also feature Lynskey as an executive producer. The series aims to dramatize the Australian true crime case surrounding Patterson.

The narrative will focus on the 97 days between a notorious 2023 lunch and Patterson’s arrest. During that meal, Patterson allegedly served toxic death cap mushrooms to her estranged in-laws, concealed within individual servings of beef wellington.
summary: Melanie Lynskey Stars and Executive Produces Paramount+ Series 'Mushroom Murders'.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Cult director Alex Cox announces final film Dead Souls
content:
Alex Cox, the cult director known for the 1984 punk classic Repo Man and the biopic Sid and Nancy, is preparing to release what he describes as his final film, Dead Souls. The new feature is a darkly comic western loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s 1842 novel of the same name. Cox invites fans to submit questions about the project and his career.

Cox’s career began with Repo Man, followed by Sid and Nancy, which starred Gary Oldman as Sid Vicious. In 1987 he directed the political western Walker, featuring Ed Harris. From 1988 to 1994 he presented BBC Two’s Moviedrome, showcasing cult and overlooked films and pioneering a form of film‑nerd programming that predated YouTube.
summary: Alex Cox, the cult director of Repo Man and Sid and Nancy, says his upcoming film Dead Souls will be his final film. Dead Souls is a darkly comic western loosely based on Nikolai Gogol’s 1842 novel.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Peven Everett documentary explores life after cancer and musical career
content: A new documentary follows the Chicagoan from child trumpet prodigy to Gabriel-singing icon and DIY maverick. ‘Not everybody wants to see musical genius’, he says At We Out Here festival in Dorset in August, thousands of people could be heard singing a trumpet melody as if it was a giant brass-band karaoke session. On stage was Peven Everett, performing a rendition of Gabriel, one of the most celebrated anthems in dance-music history. Co-created with producer Roy Davis Jr, the best-known version, which blew up in UK clubs in the mid-90s, is a spiritual garage-house track about the “archangel of love” that can bring both punters and DJs to tears. But Everett is much more than one song. Damon Albarn of Gorillaz tells me that “Peven has a once-in-a-generation voice … he’s a great inspiration to us all.” We Out Here founder, Gilles Peterson says that the Chicagoan is, alongside Detroit’s Moodymann and Amp Fiddler, “the closest thing dance music has to a Prince-type figure”. A prolific multi-instrumentalist and one-man cottage industry, Everett’s catalogue spans more than 500 tracks, across house, neo-soul, hip-hop, samba and more.
summary: A new documentary follows Chicagoan Peven Everett from child trumpet prodigy to house music icon and DIY maverick. The film examines his life after cancer and his role in vanquishing the 'Disco Sucks' movement.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Horror plays from London take over New York stage amid demand for communal experiences
content:
Horror productions are currently dominating the New York stage, driven by a surge in demand for communal experiences. Hit London plays, including 2:22, Paranormal Activity, and A Ghost in Your Ear, are now performing on and off Broadway. This trend coincides with a broader post-pandemic shift as audiences seek to escape smartphone addiction and return to in-person interactions.

The recovery of the entertainment industry supports this shift toward live, immersive events. Hollywood and Broadway box office revenues have returned to pre-pandemic levels this year, while IMAX and 4DX formats are breaking records. Additionally, concert attendance has reached new highs, and the most recently tracked season of New York theatre grossed more than the previous one. Consequently, horror, described as the most communal genre, has become the hottest ticket for the fall.
summary: Successful London productions including 2:22, Paranormal Activity, and A Ghost in Your Ear are now drawing large audiences in New York. This surge in demand for horror theater is attributed to a post-pandemic craving for in-person communal experiences.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump Midterms: 'If His Side Wins, Elections Were Honest'
content: Late-night hosts discussed Trump discrediting midterms results, and Don Jr’s friendship with a Russian oligarch Late-night hosts looked into Republicans’ efforts to discredit election results ahead of the US midterms and Donald Trump Jr ’s questionable friendship with a Putin-aligned oligarch.
summary: Late-night hosts discussed Trump's efforts to discredit midterm election results and Donald Trump Jr.'s friendship with a Putin-aligned oligarch. Jimmy Kimmel commented that if Trump's side wins the midterms, it would prove the elections were honest.

title: David Boon Named Cricket Australia Interim Chair Amid Financial Crisis
content: Australia’s former No 3 faces one of his biggest tests as he takes the reins as CA interim chair with BBL privatisation only the first task of many David Boon walked on to one of the stickier wickets in Australian sport on Wednesday, after Cricket Australia warned the national pastime faces years of financial losses and a period of “cost minimisation”. The outlook is grim, and that’s without a glance towards a cricketing world of emboldened match-fixers and upturned by Indian interests, facing an Australian summer that is no longer the country’s own. The moustached former Test No 3 batter was sent into the middle due to the ousting of Mike Baird, whose place as chair was pulled out from under him by New South Wales officials unhappy at the manner of his pursuit of BBL private investment.
summary: David Boon has taken over as the interim chair of Cricket Australia following the ousting of Mike Baird by New South Wales officials. The former Test batter now faces a difficult role as Cricket Australia warns of years of financial losses and a period of cost minimisation.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Chiefs reportedly signing Justin Tucker to practice squad after Butker struggles
content:
The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad following Harrison Butker’s recent struggles. Butker has missed five of his 16 field goal attempts this season. Tucker, who was widely regarded as one of the best kickers in NFL history, was released by the Ravens in May 2025. The team described his departure as a “football decision” due to a slump in form, though it occurred months after he was accused of inappropriate sexual behavior by massage therapists.

Tucker denied the allegations and never faced criminal charges. However, he served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league’s personal conduct policy.
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs are reportedly signing former Baltimore Ravens kicker Justin Tucker to their practice squad following Harrison Butker's poor start to the season. Tucker previously served a 10-game NFL ban for violating the league's personal conduct policy after being accused of inappropriate sexual behavior.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Qwan'tez Stiggers: From delivery driver to New York Jets player after father's death
content:
Qwan’tez Stiggers, a player for the New York Jets, recently shared his journey from working as a delivery driver to reaching the NFL. Stiggers’ football aspirations were derailed when he was 18, just days after arriving at college. Following a car crash that left him in a coma, his father died seven months later. Forced to drop out of school, Stiggers returned home to support his mother, Kwanna, and their 12 siblings.

During this difficult period, Stiggers’ then-girlfriend, Cheyenne, was also coping with the loss of her teenage sister to a stray bullet. For the next six years, the couple supported each other while Stiggers worked late-night delivery jobs and washed trucks to pay the bills. Although watching his former teammates advance in their football careers was challenging, Stiggers stated that he wanted better for himself while raising a child and living with his partner. Despite these hardships, he eventually realized his dream of playing in the NFL.
summary: Qwan'tez Stiggers dropped out of college to support his mother and 12 siblings after his father died. He worked as a delivery driver before eventually joining the New York Jets.
author: Guardian Sport

title: London Broncos to forfeit £1.3m RFL funding if joining Super League in 2027
content:
London Broncos have agreed to a condition from the existing 14 Super League clubs requiring them to relinquish rights to approximately £1.3m in central distribution funding if they enter the competition in 2027. The Rugby Football League is expected to ratify the club’s elevation imminently, marking a significant step in the expansion of Super League to 15 teams.

This development occurs as a planned partnership between Super League and Australia’s National Rugby League (NRL) is not expected to begin until 2028. The agreement would have seen the NRL take administrative control of the English game and provide tens of millions of pounds in financial support. Despite the delayed start of this partnership, the inclusion of London in the Super League has moved closer to realization.
summary: London Broncos agreed to relinquish rights to approximately £1.3m in central distribution funding as a condition for entering Super League in 2027. The Rugby Football League is expected to ratify their elevation imminently, while a partnership with the NRL is not anticipated until 2028.
author: Guardian Sport

title: West Ham's Viviane Asseyi: 'When I was four I said I wanted to be like Zidane'
content:
West Ham forward Viviane Asseyi credits the 1998 World Cup for inspiring her football dream, recalling that she declared at age four she wanted to be like Zinedine Zidane. The French player, who has a Gabonese background, has found a new family in east London while balancing her professional career.

Asseyi describes a post-match ritual where she calls her mother, who often teases her about her performance. Asseyi notes that her mother’s laughter and honest feedback help her stay motivated, emphasizing that she accepts both praise and criticism as part of her continuous effort to improve.
summary: French forward Viviane Asseyi explains that the 1998 World Cup inspired her football dream and that she has found a new family in east London. She describes a ritual of calling her mother after matches, where her mother's honest feedback helps her continue working to improve.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Marco Jansen's all-round excellence highlights lack of equivalent players in England and Australia
content:
South African cricketer Marco Jansen is highlighted as a standout all-rounder who embodies a rare combination of physical and technical attributes. Standing 6ft 8in, he possesses long limbs and a whiplash action that generates steep bounce, complemented by speed and the ability to move both ways. His left-arm delivery provides a distinct advantage, while his batting style allows him to hit sixes or adjust his approach when an innings becomes difficult. The article suggests that England and Australia are currently searching for an equivalent player to Jansen.

In the third Test, Jansen had recorded 99 Test wickets at an average of 20.81. His performance in the second Test against Australia at Gqeberha was pivotal, where he scored 85 runs to help South Africa recover from a score of 110 for six. This counterattack enabled the team to convert a precarious position into an innings victory. Although Jansen is still developing as a batter, his average of 25.66 prior to the current Test is considered an understatement of his potential.
summary: Marco Jansen, a 6ft 8in South African, has taken 99 Test wickets at 20.81 and scored 85 in the second Test against Australia. His performance demonstrates a rare combination of bowling and batting skills that England and Australia are currently seeking to replicate.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Fernandes tells Carrick he is committed to turning season around
content:
Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks with Manchester United manager Michael Carrick on Tuesday following the captain’s recent criticism of the team’s tactics. The 32-year-old met with Carrick before training at Carrington to offer assurances that he is fully committed to turning the season around. Fernandes is expected to return to the starting lineup for Saturday’s match against Chelsea.

The meeting was part of a broader effort to address tensions within the squad. Carrick also held a positive meeting with the rest of the players, during which the team made the same vow to support the manager and improve their performance.
summary: Manchester United captain Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks with manager Michael Carrick after previously criticizing the coach's tactics. Fernandes assured Carrick of his commitment to turn the team's season around and is expected to start at Chelsea on Saturday.
author: Guardian Sport

summary: Former Arsenal forward Thierry Henry responded to criticism of comments he made during Monday's Ballon d'Or ceremony. He said the remarks were intended as jokes.

title: BL Harbert International sues State Department for $461 million over embassy projects
content: BL Harbert International, an Alabama-based construction firm, filed a lawsuit against the State Department on Wednesday seeking $461 million. The company alleges the government refused to cover pandemic-era cost overruns for a dozen embassy and consulate projects. Harbert claims the government initially agreed to a settlement, but political appointees under Secretary of State Marco Rubio later intervened in the process.
summary: An Alabama-based construction company sued the State Department for refusing to pay pandemic-era cost overruns on a dozen embassy and consulate projects. BL Harbert International alleges that political appointees under Secretary of State Marco Rubio intervened after the government had agreed to a settlement.

title: Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks argue AI and climate crisis share roots in private profit
content:
Director Adam McKay and author Philip Eubanks argue that both artificial intelligence and the climate crisis share the same root cause: private entities seeking to cash in. They assert that humanity has the power to stand against these threats, ensuring that neither will end the species.

The piece highlights a summer marked by extreme heat, entire villages obliterated in Nepal, and a super El Niño breaking records. It further notes that Exxon has publicly stated that global temperatures may reach 3C by 2050, questioning if conditions could possibly be worse before introducing the threat of AI extinction.
summary: Adam McKay and Philip Eubanks state that both artificial intelligence and the climate crisis stem from private entities seeking financial gain. They assert that humanity has the power to stand against these threats, which they suggest could otherwise end the species.

title: Mark Carney centralizes power and cuts rights laws despite global praise
content:
Shiri Pasternak, an associate professor of criminology at Toronto Metropolitan University, argues that Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is facing a dual reality. Internationally, Carney is celebrated as a hero for his Davos speech, which addressed the shifting global power dynamics occurring in the shadow of Donald Trump’s presidency.

However, Pasternak contends that Carney’s domestic actions contradict this international image. She states that the Prime Minister is mirroring the US president by radically centralizing power within his office and cabinet. According to Pasternak, Carney is also dismantling dozens of laws that protect environmental, Indigenous, and labour rights to facilitate his economic agenda. Pasternak, who is also a member of the Infrastructure Beyond Extractivism research team, highlights this contrast between Carney’s external diplomatic stance and his internal political maneuvers.
summary: Mark Carney is celebrated internationally for his Davos speech addressing the reconfiguration of power under Donald Trump. However, he is simultaneously centralizing authority within his office and cabinet while repealing laws protecting environmental, Indigenous, and labour rights to advance his economic agenda.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study of 244 million Americans refines understanding of long COVID
content: An analysis of 244 million Americans has refined the understanding of long COVID, a condition where serious health effects persist after a negative coronavirus test. Patients report symptoms such as brain fog, fatigue, dizziness, rapid heart rate, shortness of breath, and chest pain. These issues affect nearly every organ system and can last for a year or more following the initial infection.
summary: Long COVID is characterized by serious health effects that persist well after a patient tests negative for coronavirus infection. Patients report symptoms such as brain fog, fatigue, and chest pain that affect nearly every organ system and last a year or more.
author: Medical Xpress

title: GP: Exercise-induced chest pain may signal specific condition
content: General practitioners note that chest pain is a symptom that often causes concern among patients, who may fear it indicates serious underlying issues with their heart or lungs.
summary: A general practitioner notes that chest pain often causes worry about serious heart or lung problems. The article suggests that exercise can trigger this pain due to a specific condition.

title: Autistic children reach ER in mental health crisis from age 8
content: Research indicates that autistic individuals face elevated risks of mental health challenges and are more prone to suicidal ideation or attempts compared to the general population.
summary: Research indicates that autistic people face higher risks of mental health difficulties than the general population. They are also more likely to think about or attempt suicide.

title: UC Santa Barbara model predicts low birth weight risk in West Africa
content: Researchers at UC Santa Barbara have developed a method to predict the likelihood of low birth weights in West Africa using climate and socioeconomic data. When integrated into an early warning system for child health, this model aims to provide decision-makers and aid organizations with sufficient time to prevent malnutrition and its subsequent effects.
summary: Researchers at UC Santa Barbara developed a method to predict low birth weight likelihood in West Africa using climate and socioeconomic data. Incorporating this model into an early warning system could allow decision-makers and aid organizations to prevent malnutrition.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study: Controlled low-oxygen exposure may alleviate Parkinson's symptoms
content:
A study conducted at São Paulo State University (UNESP) in Brazil indicates that short, controlled exposure to low-oxygen air is safe and does not interfere with sleep. The research found that this technique can modulate hormones and inflammation markers in individuals with Parkinson's disease, offering a potential benefit despite the usual physical strain associated with breathing thin air.

These preliminary results suggest that controlled inhalation of low-oxygen air may serve as a complementary therapy for Parkinson's symptoms. The findings pave the way for further research into the efficacy of this approach for managing the condition.
summary: A study by São Paulo State University found that short, controlled exposure to low-oxygen air is safe and does not interfere with sleep. The research showed that this exposure can modulate hormones and inflammation markers in people with Parkinson's disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: San Francisco estate sells for record $10m above listing price
content: An eight-bedroom mansion in San Francisco’s Presidio Heights neighborhood sold for $28.5m on 22 October, exceeding its $18.5m listing price by $10m. This transaction establishes a new record for the city, driven by rising real estate costs amid the artificial intelligence boom. The property, which features a private garden and a three-car garage, was originally listed on 2 October.
summary: San Francisco estate sells for record $10m above listing price.
author: Guardian Business

title: Fed expected to keep rates steady in final pre‑midterm meeting
content:
The U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to keep interest rates unchanged at its final rate‑setting meeting before the midterm elections, maintaining a level that is among the highest seen in more than two decades.  

Last month, the Fed raised rates for the first time since 2023, a move that angered former President Donald Trump. The decision was driven by rising inflation, which has remained above the Fed’s 2 % target for years and stayed above 3 % for most of the current year.
summary: The Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, its last rate‑setting meeting before the midterm elections. Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation that has stayed above the 2% target and above 3% for most of the year.
author: Guardian Business

title: Discovering Vasari beyond the page
content:
Most students of Renaissance art first encounter Giorgio Vasari through his book Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects. First published in 1550 and expanded in a second edition in 1568, the work is often considered the first major piece of art history. It has shaped how generations have understood artists such as Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, and Raphael.

For centuries, Vasari's reputation has rested largely on his role as the artistic biographer of the Renaissance.
summary: Discovering Vasari beyond the page.
author: Phys.org

title: You Can See Everything review: Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes film is absurd but captivating
content:
The documentary You Can See Everything, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is set for release in the US now and in the UK on 20 November. The film follows Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder of Theranos, during her final weeks before surrendering to federal prison. Fielder, a comedian known for creating elaborate scenarios with real people, moves in with Holmes, her partner Billy Evans, and their two children for the month leading up to her incarceration.

Holmes faces more than a decade in prison for falsely claiming that Theranos’s machine could perform hundreds of diagnostic tests using a single drop of blood, which defrauded investors of hundreds of millions of dollars. Despite these charges, Holmes maintains her innocence, telling Fielder she has nothing to hide and claiming she has not told a lie since childhood. However, the film suggests that her assertion that viewers can "see everything" is not accurate, as discrepancies become increasingly apparent throughout the narrative.

The film shifts its focus from Holmes to an examination of how people form perceptions of others, casting doubt on the objective recall of information, particularly when personal and professional boundaries blur. The reviewer notes that the film is difficult to categorize strictly as a documentary because Fielder appears more focused on entertainment than truth-seeking, making it hard to trust any character on screen, including Fielder himself.

Despite its absurd premise and questionable reliability, the film is described as captivating. The reviewer was engaged for almost the entire three-hour runtime, noting that Holmes ultimately "cracks" Fielder rather than the other way around. The experience left the viewer disoriented and unable to trust the conclusions presented, which the reviewer suspects was the directors' intent.
summary: The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in her final weeks before prison as Nathan Fielder moves in with her family. Although the documentary's premise is absurd, the reviewer found the three-hour runtime captivating and worth watching.
author: New Scientist

title: Sabrina Pasterski develops holographic theory to unify gravity and quantum mechanics
content: Physicist Sabrina Pasterski, frequently described as a genius, constructed and piloted her own airplane by age 16. She is currently developing a theoretical concept aimed at unifying gravity and quantum theory.
summary: Physicist Sabrina Pasterski is developing a holographic theory that could unify gravity and quantum theory. She is often described as a genius and built her own plane by the age of 16.
author: New Scientist

title: Astronomers spot possible new dwarf planet beyond Pluto
content: Astronomers have detected a potential dwarf planet in the outer solar system using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. If this object is confirmed, it would become a new member of the exclusive group of known dwarf planets.
summary: Astronomers using the Vera C. Rubin Observatory have identified an object in the outer solar system that appears to be a dwarf planet. If confirmed, the object would join the limited group of known dwarf planets.
author: New Scientist

title: Scientists link Northern ice sheets to Southern Ocean cooling, driving past ice ages
content: Scientists have identified a potential link between Earth’s poles that may explain the onset of past ice ages. New research indicates that expanding ice sheets in the Northern Hemisphere cooled Atlantic Ocean waters, which then traveled south toward Antarctica. This process may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, enabling the ocean to absorb and store more atmospheric carbon dioxide. The resulting increase in carbon sequestration likely contributed to further planetary cooling.
summary: Scientists discovered a link between expanding Northern Hemisphere ice sheets and cooling of Atlantic waters that traveled south to Antarctica. The cooling disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists uncover 100-million-year-old volcanic system in Iran
content: Scientists have uncovered a long‑lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, adding a hidden chapter to Earth’s tectonic history. The find offers new insight into the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.
summary: Scientists have uncovered a long‑lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.
author: Science Daily

title: Thwaites Glacier Melt Could Raise Sea Levels Twice Predicted
content:
Antarctica’s Thwaites Glacier is melting at twice the rate previously predicted, even without additional global warming. Scientists have found that warm ocean water penetrates miles beneath the ice, weakening its foundations and accelerating its retreat.

A new model indicates the glacier could contribute up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100. There is also a 60% probability that the glacier will lose a crucial stabilizing ridge.
summary: Scientists found that warm ocean water is penetrating miles beneath Thwaites Glacier, accelerating its retreat and weakening its foundations. A new model predicts the glacier could add up to 30 millimeters to global sea levels by 2100.
author: Science Daily

title: Smaller EV batteries, longer range? Scientists may have found a way
content: Scientists have developed a technology that could enable smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting electric vehicle batteries, potentially increasing the distance cars can travel on a single charge. By applying precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, the researchers found a method to prevent damaging lithium buildup, a factor that has previously hindered the development of next-generation batteries.
summary: Scientists have developed a new technology that could make electric vehicle batteries smaller, lighter, and longer-lasting, potentially allowing cars to travel farther on a single charge. By borrowing precision manufacturing techniques from computer chip production, they found a way to prevent damaging lithium buildup that has held back next-generation batteries.
author: Science Daily

title: AI labs buy data from dead startups to train models
content:
AI laboratories are increasingly purchasing data from defunct startups to train their models, a trend driven by the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Keelan Miskell, who wound down his crypto startup, sold the company’s codebase and workspace data for tens of thousands of dollars. This growing market involves companies that assist in shutting down startups selling their digital archives to AI labs seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. These sales have raised legal and ethical questions regarding the use of such data.

In a separate feature titled “Are we there yet?”, the newsletter explores the progress of interspecies communication. The article notes that humans are not the only species with communication abilities and that decoding animal communication could reveal the inner lives of other species. Advances in AI and a growing arsenal of devices have made it easier to study animal sounds, such as howls, squeaks, and clicks, although making sense of this data remains complex. The story is part of a series that evaluates six technologies on a progress meter.

The newsletter also highlights a narrated podcast episode discussing the challenges of building a city on the moon. The US and China are racing to build lunar bases, with NASA aiming to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. The moon’s hostile environment presents significant obstacles, including falling asteroids, cosmic radiation, sharp lunar dust, and extreme temperature swings. A sprawling base would require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and the use of lunar resources for self-sustainability, though political will may be the chief obstacle.

The “must-reads” section summarizes several key technology stories. Hackers disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website a week before the midterms, hiding spending data during what is described as the costliest midterms ever. Additionally, restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine have driven US allies to rethink their dependence on the service, spooking European officials and providing a pitch for rival services. Greenhouse gas levels, including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, are reaching new records worldwide.

Other notable stories include Chinese scientists developing a catalyst to convert Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide into liquid methanol for rocket fuel. Tech billionaires, including Sergey Brin and Eric Schmidt, have funded a major campaign against California’s wealth tax. Delaware is planning to allow AI agents to run entire businesses, a proposal that could let owners evade responsibility for harm. Furthermore, Palmer Luckey has unveiled plans for Anduril to build rugged, American-made military laptops in Ohio using Qualcomm chips.

The newsletter concludes with a quote from Matthew Prince, Cloudflare’s chief executive, who stated that for the next two years, there will be a critical, internet-wide vulnerability every week on average, as AI finds software vulnerabilities faster than they can be patched. A final article examines Apple’s strategy to become net zero by the end of the decade by planting millions of eucalyptus trees in Brazil, a move critics warn may do more harm than good.
summary: AI labs are purchasing codebases and workspace data from shut-down startups to train models as public and synthetic datasets reach their limits. This growing market raises legal and ethical questions regarding the use of data from failed companies.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: England Judge Geoffrey Vos Supports AI Adjudication of Civil Cases
content:
England’s top judge Geoffrey Vos says AI could adjudicate many civil cases.  

He notes the challenge lies in defining where the line should be drawn.
summary: England judge Geoffrey Vos believes AI could adjudicate many civil cases. He says the main issue is determining where to draw the line.

content: The latest generation of Amazon’s 7-inch Kindle e-readers, including the 2026 Paperwhite and Colorsoft models, features a new design and updated accessories. A review examines whether these devices justify an upgrade considering Amazon’s revised Kindle pricing.
summary: The latest generation of Kindle’s 7‑inch e‑readers, including the Paperwhite 2026 and Colorsoft 2026, feature a new look and new accessories. The review questions whether the upgrades are worth the new Kindle prices.
